props.title: Devil

sections.content: Devil kicked off M. Night Shyamalan's "Night Chronicles" with a claustrophobic thriller that traps five strangers in an elevator with sinister consequences. The film draws from Christian mythology and follows the "locked room mystery" tradition established by classics like 12 Angry Men (1957). Its confined setting amplifies tension similar to Phone Booth (2002) and Buried (2010), where limited space becomes a pressure cooker for human nature's darker impulses.

sections.content: The elevator-as-hell metaphor in Devil taps into a rich vein of supernatural confined-space horror. 1408 (2007) traps its protagonist in a haunted hotel room, while Autopsy of Jane Doe (2016) confines its terror to a morgue basement. These settings force characters to confront both external threats and their own moral failings, a theme Devil explores through its reveal of each character's past sins.

The film's religious undertones connect it to a wave of supernatural horror that includes The Exorcism of Emily Rose (2005) and Sinister (2012). However, Devil distinguishes itself by combining theological elements with the whodunit structure of And Then There Were None (1945), creating a unique hybrid of mystery and supernatural horror. SUBHEAD: The Confined Space Thriller Evolution

sections.content: Devil's success helped popularize the single-location thriller format, paving the way for films like Locke (2013) and The Guilty (2018). The format proves especially effective for building sustained tension through character dynamics rather than relying on elaborate set pieces. This approach influenced later works like The Belko Experiment (2016) and Oxygen (2021), which similarly explore human nature under extreme confinement.
